English Wikipedia, 'Hubert Wilkins' (read for orientation and to locate the independent sources below). Not used as support for any row or card.

Mark Piesing, 'What Made the Lockheed Vega Such a Great Polar Explorer?', Air & Space Quarterly, National Air and Space Museum (Smithsonian), 30 September 2026 (read in full; draws on the Wilkins biographer Jeff Maynard and museum curators). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the 1926 Detroit-sponsored flights that ended in wrecked Fokkers and a Stinson forced down on the sea ice, the switch to a single Lockheed Vega, the 15 April 1928 flight from Point Barrow to Spitsbergen (about 2,200 miles in some 20 hours, the first airplane crossing of the Arctic Ocean, which found sea ice and no land in the unexplored area), the four days trapped on Deadman's Island and the hand-dug runway, the knighthood, the Wilkins-Hearst Antarctic Expedition with the first powered flight in Antarctica on 16 November 1928 and a 600-mile survey flight of Graham Land on 20 December, the failed plan to fly on to the Ross Sea when the Deception Island runway melted, his Military Cross and bar, his request that General Monash not nominate him for the Victoria Cross, and his weather-station ambition. A museum feature that is admiring in tone.

Burt M. McConnell, 'Sir Hubert Wilkins', Encyclopedia Arctica vol. 15 (Biographies), unpublished reference work 1947-51, Rauner Special Collections, Dartmouth (read in full). A colleague's biography: McConnell served on the Canadian Arctic Expedition with Wilkins, so it is a first-hand witness for 1913-16 (Wilkins repairing a motorboat engine, taking his turn as cook, taking no part in the staff protest at Nome, staying loyal to Stefansson's ice journey, wintering on Banks Island, walking to Coronation Gulf for the schooner) and a secondhand summary afterwards (Balkan war films, Western Front, the Quest, the two-year British Museum collecting expedition with more than 5,000 specimens, the 1925 Detroit proposal, the 1927 forced landing and the 13-day walk ashore, the 1928 navigation preparations and flight, the Antarctic flights, the Nautilus, the 1937-38 search for Levanevsky). Admiring, written by an associate of Stefansson's circle; it also records that some Antarctic 'channels' reported in 1928 proved to be glaciers.

History Trust of South Australia, Sir Hubert Wilkins Project, timeline pages '1888-1916: Early Life and Cinematography', '1917-1919: Cameraman at the Western Front' and '1926-1931: Polar Aviator and Submariner' (all read in full). A state history museum's account with quotations from Wilkins's own writing: the Balkan war filming in 1912, the Canadian Arctic Expedition and how he learned to travel light from the Inuit, the Western Front work with Bean (the Military Cross for bringing wounded back from No Man's Land), the Detroit expedition and its crashes, the 1928 flights, Hearst's sponsorship of the submarine, the 'mutinous crew', and how he put his entire savings into the Nautilus and was financially ruined and immediately looked for new sponsors. Its statement that the Military Cross bar was for a charge on a machine-gun nest differs from the Australian War Memorial's account.

Australian War Memorial, 'Hubert Wilkins (1888-1958)' (Focus: photographers) and 'Captured in colour: George Hubert Wilkins 1888-1958' (both read in full). A national memorial's account of his work as official photographer: appointed in August 1917 after colour-blindness kept him from flying, 'famous for his bravery and recklessness' on the battlefield, the first person to film combat in the 1912 Balkan war, two Military Crosses (the first for bringing in wounded under fire, the bar for leading inexperienced American troops out of a deadly situation in September 1918), more than two years at the front, and the 1919 Gallipoli mission with Bean.

American Philosophical Society Library, online exhibition 'Low Road North: Sir Hubert Wilkins's 1931 Polar Expedition' (exhibition page and the 'History of the Expedition' page read in full; built on the scrapbook of the Nautilus's chief electrician Frank Blumberg). The Nautilus voyage: the plan agreed with Lincoln Ellsworth, the former U.S. Navy O-12 refitted and renamed, the start two months behind schedule under mounting criticism, the engine failures and tow by USS Wyoming, the lost diving rudders and the suspicion of sabotage tied to some crew's lack of confidence in Wilkins, his determination to carry out the science anyway, the first dives beneath a three-foot floe on 31 August, his being persuaded that it was no longer safe, and the scuttling on 20 November 1931. Says a late start and repeated mechanical problems prevented the Pole.

Encyclopedia of Australian Science and Innovation, 'Wilkins, George Hubert' (Swinburne University of Technology and University of Melbourne eScholarship; read in full). An institutional chronology that gives dated posts (Gaumont cameraman 1908-12, Canadian Arctic Expedition second-in-command 1913-16, Military Cross and bar 1918, naturalist on the Quest 1921-22, the 1923-25 British Museum collecting in tropical Australia, the 1928 trans-Arctic flight and knighthood, aerial Antarctic expeditions 1928-39, the 1931 submarine attempt, wartime consulting for the U.S. Army) and lists the biographies (Grierson 1960, Nasht 2006, the Australian Dictionary of Biography entry by Swan).

Jeff Maynard, 'Australia's unsung hero', Australian Geographic, 11 January 2024 (read in full). A magazine essay by Wilkins's biographer (the same informant as the National Air and Space Museum feature, so not independent of it): General Monash naming him the bravest man under his command and calling him 'aggressively modest' when he asked not to be put up for the Victoria Cross, his refusal to carry a gun, nine Antarctic visits, the mutinous Nautilus crew, his ruin after 1931, the Australian government's refusal in 1939 to back his Antarctic plan at Mawson's urging, and the author's own warning that biographers meet conflicting information and fanciful tales about him. Used for context and for the limits of the evidence.

persistence.rationale: [src_wilkins_nasm, src_wilkins_mcconnell, src_wilkins_aps, src_wilkins_historytrust | 1926-1931 | museum feature, colleague biography, society library exhibition, state museum timeline] After the 1926 Fokker and Stinson crashes and the 1927 forced landing and walk ashore he came back in 1928 with a single Vega (NASM, McConnell); on Deadman's Island the pair dug a runway by hand and tried repeatedly to take off (NASM); on the Nautilus, with the diving rudders gone and the Pole out of reach, he carried on with the science and the first ice dives (APS, McConnell); and after the 1931 ruin he at once sought sponsors for another submarine attempt (History Trust). Four sources describe separate episodes. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 82 / 0.70 because the NASM feature and the Australian Geographic essay share one biographer, McConnell is an associate who also leans on Wilkins's own reports, and some of the Nautilus crew thought the voyage a suicide mission (APS). RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 78@0.66 -> 74@0.6. the 1926-28 retries are documented but the museum feature, society exhibition and colleague biography retell one narrative.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_wilkins_awm, src_wilkins_historytrust, src_wilkins_nasm, src_wilkins_mcconnell, src_wilkins_aps, src_wilkins_ageo | 1912-1931 | national war memorial, state museum timeline, museum feature, colleague biography, society library exhibition, biographer's magazine essay] He filmed the 1912 Balkan fighting from the front, often went over the top with the troops while refusing to carry a gun, and won the Military Cross for bringing wounded men in from No Man's Land (AWM, History Trust, NASM, Australian Geographic); in 1927 and 1928 he flew over unmapped ice with fuel running out or into a storm over Spitsbergen (NASM, McConnell); and he staked all his savings on a refitted 1916 submarine (History Trust, APS). The cost was real (a ruined expedition fund, a mutinous crew), hence dual-edged. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 84 / 0.72 because the war-service accounts repeat one set of award descriptions (and the two institutions differ on what the bar was for), and the flight dangers are mostly told in his own reports. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 80@0.66 -> 76@0.6. NASM and Australian Geographic share one biographer and several episodes are retold from Wilkins's own accounts; outcome bias in survivorship-framed accounts.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_wilkins_mcconnell, src_wilkins_historytrust, src_wilkins_nasm | 1913-1928 | colleague biography, state museum timeline, museum feature] McConnell reports that he repaired a motorboat plant that had defeated the ship's engineer, built what Stefansson called the most comfortable winter base though he had no experience, and in 1927 improvised sleds from the ski and cowling and dried his frozen trousers in powder snow; the History Trust says he learned from the Inuit to travel light, and NASM has him hiring men to clear runways and digging one by hand in 1928. Most of the improvising is told by one colleague. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.62 because the Canadian Arctic details rest on McConnell, who quotes Stefansson's praise, and the 1927 account also comes from Wilkins's own report.

adaptability.rationale: [src_wilkins_mcconnell, src_wilkins_historytrust, src_wilkins_nasm | 1913-1931 | colleague biography, state museum timeline, museum feature] Stefansson, quoted by McConnell, wrote that Wilkins had 'proved as adaptable to polar conditions as any man I ever saw', and the History Trust says he learned from the Inuit and adjusted to the environment; after losing most of his photographic gear with the Karluk he carried on (McConnell); when the Fokkers failed he switched to a single Vega, and after flying the Arctic he turned to a submarine (NASM, History Trust). Several distinct adjustments are documented, though the praise is partly one colleague's quotation. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.60 because the headline adaptability quote is Stefansson's, relayed by McConnell.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_wilkins_mcconnell, src_wilkins_historytrust, src_wilkins_nasm, src_wilkins_eoas | 1916-1930 | colleague biography, state museum timeline, museum feature, institutional chronology] He left the Canadian expedition in 1916 to get to the war, enlisted for flying and asked for a pilot's role (McConnell, AWM, History Trust), led the British Museum's two-year collecting expedition (EOAS, McConnell), and organised the Wilkins-Hearst Antarctic Expedition and obtained Hearst's sponsorship for the submarine (NASM, History Trust). The sources disagree on who started the Detroit venture (McConnell says he convinced the Detroit businessmen, the History Trust says Stefansson brought him the offer). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.60 because the origin of the Detroit expedition is told two ways and McConnell is again the main witness for the early initiatives. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 72@0.58 -> 70@0.54. initiative episodes depend on a colleague biography and one museum timeline; the 1916 departure is a single-source anecdote.

curiosity.rationale: [src_wilkins_mcconnell, src_wilkins_eoas, src_wilkins_aps, src_wilkins_nasm | 1913-1931 | colleague biography, institutional chronology, society library exhibition, museum feature] McConnell says he took an interest in all branches of scientific work on the Canadian expedition, wrote up bird observations from the Quest for Ibis and led a two-year collecting trip that, per the Museum director's report he cites, brought back more than 5,000 specimens (EOAS lists plants, birds, insects, fish, minerals and fossils); in 1927 he stopped on the ice to take a deep-water sounding, and the Nautilus carried a gravity, oceanographic and magnetic programme (McConnell, APS). A curator quoted by NASM calls him curious and open to other cultures. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.56 because the specimen count and the Ibis reports come from McConnell alone and the curator's remark is one comment.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_wilkins_mcconnell, src_wilkins_nasm, src_wilkins_aps | 1922-1931 | colleague biography, museum feature, society library exhibition] On one side, McConnell says he worked through simulated great-circle navigation problems for days before the 1928 flight and presented a polar weather-station plan to the Royal Meteorological Society in 1922; on the other, the 1926 Fokkers were wrecked within days of arriving, and the 1931 Nautilus left two months behind schedule with engines that had stood idle for years and failed in the Atlantic (NASM, APS). The evidence points both ways. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 58 / 0.44 because the navigation preparation is a single colleague's account while the Nautilus delays are well documented.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_wilkins_nasm, src_wilkins_mcconnell | 1922-1948 | museum feature, colleague biography] NASM and McConnell both report that watching drought ruin his family's South Australian farm led him to want a ring of polar weather stations for long-range forecasting; McConnell says he put a plan to the Royal Meteorological Society in 1922, which was thought premature and was not taken up until some 26 years later, and that he later advised the U.S. Weather Bureau. The motive comes from his own account as retold by both. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.46 because the stated motive is self-report relayed by two accounts that share the same origin.

The print bears a handwritten white copyright mark reading approximately 'Hillwilliams, N.Y.'; the Library lists no creator. The file is the Library's 4083 x 5120 master scan cropped to the print and downscaled to 800 x 1000 with no upscaling.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead) / REPLACED with a sibling item. The lead, Commons 'Hubert Wilkins 1931.jpg', is Library of Congress item 2002721458 (cph.3a23921, 'created/published 1931', creator not named); the Library's own record says 'Rights status not evaluated' and 'This record contains unverified, old data from caption card', and the Commons tag PD-USGov is a wrong basis for a non-government photograph, so the lead is unusable as a rights-clear item even though the print itself carries a handwritten 'Sir Hubert Wilkins'. REPLACEMENT: the other Library of Congress print, item 2002721457 (cph.3a53251, shown on Commons as 'Hubert Wilkins 1926.jpg', also tagged PD-USGov there, which is wrong): holder record gives title 'George Hubert Wilkins', date 'c1926 Jan. 8', note 'J280722 U.S. Copyright Office', rights 'No known restrictions on publication', and a caution that the data come from an old caption card. The real basis is expired U.S. copyright: a work whose copyright was secured under the 1909 Act in 1926 had a 95-year maximum term and is public domain since 2022. I used the Library's master TIFF (4083 x 5120), cropped to the print and downscaled to 800 x 1000. IDENTITY: not carried by lettering on this print; it rests on the Library's caption, on the matching hairline, ears, brow and beard of the Library's 1931 print that is handwritten 'Sir Hubert Wilkins' and of the Australian War Memorial 1922 portrait, and on a Seattle Post-Intelligencer glass negative of about 1926 handwritten 'Capt. Geo. H. Wilkins' showing the same beard and fur parka (a rights-conflicted image, used only for comparison); the 1926 date fits his first Detroit Arctic expedition. Holder-rights caveats on rejected alternatives: Australian War Memorial P03171.002 and .003 say 'copyright expired - public domain' but add that copies and permission can only be obtained from Ohio State University (Byrd Polar archive), and the sitting dates differ (c1922 and c1918), so not used; Canadian Museum of History negative 38747 (Anderson, 1915, on Commons as CC BY-SA 4.0) sits in a record family whose rights field says to consult the archives staff, so not used; the Seattle MOHAI negative is credited 'All Rights Reserved'; State Library of NSW FL1659835 (Underwood and Underwood, 1930) returns HTTP 403 to automated access (bot wall, not a rights conflict) and was not opened; the Bundesarchiv 1928 image is a group shot; the National Portrait Gallery's 1933 Irving Browning print is copyright-restricted. KIND likeness: a studio photograph of his face. Date 'c1926' is the copyright date, not a verified sitting date. His First World War official-photographer service (the Military Cross) is scored only as risk-taking in the field; his OSS and U.S. Army consulting in the Second World War, the 1937-38 Levanevsky search for the Soviet government, his stated opinions on civilisation and his telepathy experiments are context only and unscored. KO NAME 휴버트 윌킨스 is the Wikidata label. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated flights, expedition records, wartime service records). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Mark Piesing, Air & Space Quarterly (Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum), 2026. READ (7 substantive sources besides Wikidata and Wikipedia, 9 sources listed): NASM feature (full); McConnell in Encyclopedia Arctica (full); History Trust of South Australia timeline pages (3); Australian War Memorial pages (2); American Philosophical Society Nautilus exhibition (2 pages); EOAS entry; Australian Geographic essay by Maynard. Also read and not cited: a Naval Submarine League essay by a midshipman on the 1931 voyage (an undergraduate paper with errors such as 'wounded nine times'), the National Portrait Gallery label, the Library of Congress records. NOT OPENED: the Australian Dictionary of Biography entry (the site returned only a loading shell), Nasht's 'The Last Explorer', Grierson 1960, Wilkins's own books, the Byrd Polar archive. PERSPECTIVES: (1) museum feature drawing on his biographer (NASM, Australian Geographic); (2) a Stefansson-circle colleague's first-hand and later summary (McConnell); (3) a state museum's biographical project (History Trust); (4) a national war memorial (AWM); (5) a learned-society library's crew-scrapbook exhibition on the Nautilus (APS). NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: all of the above; the quotations from Wilkins's own writings in the History Trust pages and the 1927 and 1928 flight details retold by McConnell and NASM rest in part on his own reports. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: NASM places the Stinson crash on the sea ice in 1926, McConnell dates the forced landing to March 1927 (the year 1927 is the accepted one and is not stated in the rows); the History Trust says the Military Cross bar was for a charge on a machine-gun nest while the AWM says it was for leading American troops out of a deadly situation; the EOAS chronology and an AWM item note call him second-in-command or deputy leader of the Canadian expedition while the History Trust and NASM call him its photographer; some early Antarctic 'channels' were glaciers (McConnell); Maynard warns of fanciful tales and secrecy; the Australian Geographic essay says Mawson urged the Australian government not to back his 1939 plan (context only). No adversarial biography was read; the closest counter-voices are the APS Nautilus account of crew distrust and sabotage suspicion and the History Trust's 'mutinous crew'. CONCENTRATION: 5 rows lowered for source-family concentration (persistence, resourcefulness, proactive_agency, curiosity, impact_motivation); risk_tolerance, adaptability and planning_orientation lowered in self-calibration on other grounds. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: cards (1) the first airplane crossing of the Arctic Ocean in 1928, (2) the first Antarctic flights and survey of Graham Land 1928-30, (3) the 1931 Nautilus attempt to travel under the Arctic ice.
